steps.caption: Before balancing, District 4 is furthest from Colorado's ideal, so its border is checked first. These 24 blocks are one stretch of that border, where it meets District 3, 5.2 km from the first move, picked because all three checks show up here.
The 12 outlined blocks are on that border: District 4 blocks touching District 3, and District 3 blocks touching District 4. Each could move to the other side.
A block may move only if it has people. 1 of them has no people.
A move must narrow the gap between the two districts, here 174 people. Here 4 moves would take people from District 3 into District 4, which already has more, so they would widen it.
District 4 must stay one connected piece. Without either of these 2 blocks it would split, cutting off the 2 dotted blocks, so they stay.
That leaves 5 allowed moves here, all into District 3. Along District 4's whole border, 105 of 546 moves are allowed.
Colorado's ideal is 721,714.25 people per district. Each bar is how far a district is from it before balancing: above the line is over, below is under.
Distance counts either way. District 4 is 185.75 over and District 2 is 175.25 under, so District 4 is further.
District 4 goes first. The first real move takes 74 people out of District 4 and into District 3.
If two districts are exactly as far, the lower number goes first. Hawaii's two districts are each 35.50 people from its ideal of 727,635.50, one over and one under, so District 1 goes first.
Colorado has 5,773,714 people and 8 seats.
5,773,714 / 8 = 721,714.25 people per district, which no district can hit exactly.
So the target is the two neighbouring whole numbers: 721,714 and 721,715. Each bar is a district's final distance from the ideal, and 7 of 8 are within one person of it.
Each bar is a district's distance from Colorado's ideal of 721,714.25, before move 19 (left) and move 20 (right). Before move 19, District 1 is furthest, 2.25 under, so it is tried first.
None of the 846 moves on its border is allowed: 219 are blocks with no people and 627 would widen a gap.

Districts 2, 3 and 5 border it, larger by 3, 1 and 1 people. A move narrows a gap only if it carries fewer people than the gap, but the smallest blocks with people that could cross into it hold 16, 2 and 2.
So the pass tries the next furthest district. Districts 4 and 6 are each 1.75 over, and the lower number, District 4, goes first.
District 4 has 6 allowed moves. The best moves 1 person out of District 4 into District 3: that is move 19.
After every move the pass starts again from the furthest district. Before move 20, that is District 1 again, 2.25 under, still with no allowed move, so District 6, the next furthest, makes move 20.
In Colorado, District 4 is 185.75 over the ideal of 721,714.25 and District 3 is 11.75 over. These are the 24 blocks nearest the block that moves first.
The 5 outlined blocks may move from District 4 into District 3. Each move is scored by how much it lowers the sum of the squared differences from the ideal.
Of these, 2 tie at 13,338. A tie goes to the block that comes first in GEOID order, 080470138012017, so it ranks ahead.
The best is this block of 74 people: 2 × 74 × (185.75 − 11.75 − 74) = 14,800. The next best allowed move anywhere on District 4's border scores 14,560.
So it moves into District 3. District 4 now has 721,826 people and District 3 has 721,800, and the sum falls by exactly 14,800.
Before balancing, Colorado's districts run from 721,539 to 721,900 people, a range of 361. Squaring each district's distance from the ideal 721,714.25 and adding up gives 81,747.50.
Each of the 20 moves lowers that sum, the first by 14,800 and the last by 4. Each dot is the sum after a move.
After 20 moves the sum is 7.50 and the range is 3.
No move lowers the sum any further, so the pass stops. It always does: every move lowers the sum by at least 4, and a sum of squares never goes below zero.
Alabama has 7 seats, so its first cut splits them 3 and 4. Take the direction cut 1 used, 85.0° from north-south.
First with the 3 seats north of the line and 4 south: the line falls here, and its border is 479,246 m long.
Then the same direction with the 3 seats south of the line and 4 north: the line moves, and its border is 642,462 m long.
The shorter way is kept, with the 3 seats north of the line: 479,246 m against 642,462 m.
Colorado, small in the middle, on a plain grid of longitude and latitude, with the parallel at 39° north and the meridian at 106° west running through it.
This is cut 3's guide line, continued past the state along its great circle for 2,500 km each way. On this grid it bows: its middle sits 401 km off the straight path between its ends.
The generator measures directions in a flat projection centered on the state. In it every great circle, the path a plane through the Earth's center traces on the surface, is a straight line.
Here the guide line is exactly straight, and so is the meridian, which is also a great circle. The parallel is not a great circle, so it curves.
Cut 3 in Colorado, near the middle of its line. Every block is now on the first side or the second, shaded by side.
The border is every block edge with a first-side block on one hand and a second-side block on the other. These 15 edges measure 503 m.
Adding the next 15 edges brings it to 745 m.
All 43 border edges in view add up to 1,000 m, each measured along the surface of the Earth.
Along the whole line, 435 such edges add up to 19,258 m. That is the length of cut 3's border. Water inside the state counts as part of the state, so a bay or lake would not shorten this border.
Cut 3 in Colorado splits a piece of 23,345 blocks. These are the 20 blocks nearest the middle of its line.
Each block has an internal point, a spot inside it that the Census Bureau publishes.
What orders the blocks is how far each point sits across the line, measured at right angles to it.
Sorted by that distance, these 20 line up like this. In the full walk they fall between places 13,174 and 13,505.
The walk adds up people in this order. 13 of these blocks come before it stops and join the first side; the other 7 start the second side.
No two of the 23,345 blocks sit at exactly the same distance. If two did, the one with the smaller GEOID would come first.

Mississippi's first cut tries 1,800 straight lines, one every 0.1° from 0° to 179.9°. Each line is first settled for stray pieces, and only then is its real border measured. Each tick is that measured length.
Settling cannot fix every line. For 220 of the 1,800, the two sides are still not each one connected piece. They are marked.
Now the lines are sorted by border length, shortest first.
The shortest line, 86.4° at 363.3 km, is one of the unresolved ones. It is skipped.
The next line, 85.7° at 365.5 km, has two connected sides, so it is the cut. It is the 85.7° and 365,513 m of cut 1 on the real map.
Alabama has 5,024,279 people and 7 seats, so the first cut works on all 7.
The 7 seats split into 3 and 4. The 3-seat side should hold 3 of every 7 people.
5,024,279 x 3 / 7 = 2,153,262.43, the number of people the 3-seat side should hold.
Searching every cut in all 50 states: in 11 of 385 cuts the two shortest settled borders agree to the meter. The one on the fewest blocks is New Jersey's cut 8.
New Jersey's cut 8 splits 3 seats. Its two shortest borders run at 18.7° and 18.8°.
Both borders are 68,797.11 m, which is 6,879,711 cm. They agree to the nearest centimeter, so they are tied.
A tie goes to the line closest to north-south. 18.7° leans 18.7° from north-south and 18.8° leans 18.8°, so 18.7° goes first. Of the 11 such cuts in the data, 11 are settled by this first rule.
So the cut is the line at 18.7°. On the real map, New Jersey cut 8 is 18.7° and 68,797 m.
Cut 3 in Colorado: the first side's share is 721,581 people. Walking in order, the first 13,376 blocks add up to 721,543, still short.
Next in the walk is this block, with 147 people.
With it the total is 721,690, past the share, so the walk stops at this block.
Before it the total is 38 short of the share; after it, 109 over. After is not strictly closer, so the block starts the second side.
The guide line on the map sits halfway between the last block of the first side and the first block of the second, measured across the line.
Run the generator on Colorado and fingerprint the plan with SHA-256.
Run it again from scratch and fingerprint that plan too.
The two fingerprints are identical, so the two plans are identical.
Two blocks in Colorado, the first pair in GEOID order that touch only at a corner: 080010078011000 and 080010078011012.
They meet at this single point and share no edge. Touching at a corner does not count, so these two are not connected.
This block, 080010078011001, shares an edge with the first one, marked along its length, so those two are connected.
A line tried for cut 1 in Colorado, 133.9° from north-south. Its strays take 6 passes to settle; each dot is a block that moves in one of them.
Pass 1. After the walk, 12 blocks are cut off from their side and move, each fixed at once. 5 of them are highlighted here, close up.
Pass 2. The re-count walks the free blocks again, and 3 more blocks are cut off. 1 of them is highlighted here, close up. Dots mark blocks fixed earlier.
Pass 3. The re-count walks the free blocks again, and 1 more block is cut off. It is highlighted here, close up. Dots mark blocks fixed earlier.
Pass 4. The re-count walks the free blocks again, and 1 more block is cut off. It is highlighted here, close up. Dots mark blocks fixed earlier.
Pass 5. The re-count walks the free blocks again, and 1 more block is cut off. It is highlighted here, close up. Dots mark blocks fixed earlier.
Pass 6 moves no free block, so it ends: 6 walks, 18 fixed blocks, and the line slid 7 meters in all. A piece of 140,345 blocks could need at most 140,345 walks.
Cut 1 in Colorado, just after its first walk. These 2 blocks are on the first side, cut off from the rest of it.
They join the second side, the side around them, and are fixed to it at once. A dot marks each fixed block.
The re-count walks the free blocks again. By position these 2 would fall on the first side, but fixed blocks are left out of the walk, so they stay on the second side.
No later pass can move them either. They end cut 1 on the second side, where they were fixed.

Fixed blocks count toward their side's groups like any other block. On a line tried for cut 1 at 4.3°, this group on the second side holds 1 block fixed there (dotted) and 2 blocks still free, and it is cut off from the side's main body.
Its free blocks join the first side. Its fixed block stays on the second side, where it was fixed.
Alaska has 49 pieces of land that share no edge with the rest: islands and other detached land. This island is 2 blocks.
The nearest block of the main body is 17.3 km away, measured between internal points.
The two blocks are joined as if they shared an edge, so the island counts as connected to the rest of Alaska.
Every detached piece is joined to the nearest block of the land already joined, sometimes another island, so Alaska can be cut like any other state.
A line tried for cut 1 in Colorado, 1.8° from north-south. After its first walk, these 3 blocks are on the second side, cut off from it.
They join the first side, the side around them, and are fixed there. A dot marks each fixed block.
After the re-count, 2 free blocks here are on the other side, and these 3 are cut off from the first side.
Pass 3 moves no free block, and these 3 cannot move back: they are fixed. The first side is left in more than one piece.
So this line's first side is not one connected piece. It fails that check, and the next shortest line is considered.
Cut 2 in Colorado splits this piece, with 4 seats, into 2 and 2. The outline is the edge of the piece's blocks.
Its line runs here, 175.3° from north-south.
The line crosses the piece's outline 4 times, marked: it leaves the piece and comes back in. At this scale some of the marks sit almost on top of each other.
Up close: the line leaves the piece, runs 2.4 km outside it (dashed), and comes back in.
That is allowed. A line may cross the piece's outline any number of times.
Cut 1 in Colorado, just after its first walk. These 3 blocks are on the second side, cut off from the rest of it.
They join the first side and are fixed there with their 162 people. With 1 more block fixed elsewhere, 250 people are fixed on the first side.
The first side's share is 2,886,857 people. The 250 fixed people already count on it.
So the re-count walks the free blocks only, in the same order, toward 2,886,857 minus 250: a target of 2,886,607.
The walk stops by the same rule, and the guide line moves to halfway between the last free block of each side: here by 1 meter.
Cut 1 in Colorado, just after its first walk, shaded by side. These 2 blocks are on the first side, but no edge links them to the rest of it.
After the walk the first side is in 6 connected groups. Its main body is the group with the most people: 2,886,351 in 73,507 blocks.
This group has 324 people in 2 blocks, so it is not the main body. The block count, and then the lowest GEOID, would only decide a tie in people.
Every group other than the main body joins the second side, the side around it: here 5 groups with 6 blocks, this one included.
Then the second side is settled the same way, and 2 groups with 4 blocks cut off from it join the first side. This repeats until nothing moves.
